title: When should a component be a Server Component vs Client Component?
description: Master the Server Component mental model in Next.js App Router. Learn boundary placement, data-fetching strategy, and how to avoid common RSC pitfalls.

data.text: React Server Components (RSC) represent a fundamental shift: components can now render exclusively on the server, producing serialized props for the client without shipping JavaScript. The question every senior React engineer must answer is: **where does each component belong?** Get this wrong and you ship unnecessary JS, block streaming, or create RSC boundaries that leak interactivity.

In Next.js App Router, components are Server Components by default. Add `'use client'` at the top to opt into Client Component status. This directive creates a **boundary**: everything imported by a Client Component (and everything it renders) becomes part of the client bundle. The boundary is sticky—it flows downward, not upward.

terms.definition: A component that renders only on the server. Its output is serialized to a special format and streamed to the client. No JavaScript is shipped for its logic.
A component marked with 'use client'. It runs in the browser, can use state/effects/event handlers, and ships its JS to the client.
The subtree that starts at a Client Component and includes everything it imports and renders. Everything inside ships JS to the browser.
Sending HTML to the browser progressively as Server Components finish rendering, rather than waiting for the entire page.

data.title: Server or Client?
items: Does the component need `useState`, `useEffect`, or browser APIs? → Client Component
Does it read from `localStorage`, `window`, or `document`? → Client Component
Does it add event listeners (`onClick`, `onChange`)? → Client Component
Does it fetch data or access backend resources directly? → Server Component (default)
Does it render static UI from database content? → Server Component
Does it wrap Client Components but has no interactivity itself? → Server Component that imports client children

data.text: Pattern: Server Component as layout wrapper

data.title: Server Component fetching data, Client Component for interactivity
data.content: The page is a Server Component that fetches data and passes it to a Client Component for the interactive parts.

cards.title: Server Component
cards.description: Renders on the server, streams HTML, ships zero JS for its logic.
pros: Zero JavaScript shipped for the component's logic
Direct access to backend resources (DB, filesystem, env vars)
cons: Cannot use state, effects, or browser APIs
Every request runs server code (cost, latency)

cards.title: Client Component
cards.description: Opts into browser execution. Use only when interactivity or browser APIs are required.
pros: Full React client capabilities: state, effects, refs
Can handle events and browser APIs
Can use React hooks for client-side logic
cons: JS ships to the client—impacts bundle size
Boundary pulls in all children into the client bundle

data.title: Default to Server Components
data.text: The mental model is inverted from classic React. Instead of asking 'should this be a Client Component?', ask 'does this **need** to be a Client Component?' The answer is yes only if it uses state, effects, event handlers, or browser APIs. Everything else should stay on the server.

data.title: What goes wrong
items: Adding `'use client'` to a top-level layout pulls the entire app tree into the client bundle
Importing a Client Component into a Server Component is fine, but importing a Server Component into a Client Component is an error
Fetching data in a Client Component with `useEffect` instead of letting the Server Component handle it
Using context providers in Server Components—they require Client Components to consume

items.question: Can a Server Component import a Client Component?
items.answer: Yes. Server Components can import and render Client Components, passing serialized props. This is the standard pattern: Server Component handles data fetching, Client Component handles interactivity.

items.question: Can a Client Component import a Server Component?
items.answer: No. Server Components cannot be imported into Client Components because their code never ships to the browser. If you need this pattern, pass the Server Component's output as children or props from the Server Component.

items.question: What about context providers? Do they need 'use client'?
items.answer: Yes. Any component that uses `createContext` and a provider with state must be a Client Component. Server Components can't maintain client-side state to provide.

items.question: How does streaming interact with React Suspense?
items.answer: Suspense boundaries in Server Components let you stream content progressively. The shell renders immediately while heavy child components stream in. This improves TTFB and perceived performance without client-side JavaScript.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Default is Server Component. Add 'use client' only when you need state, effects, or events
Client Component boundaries pull in all children into the JS bundle
Pass data from Server to Client via serialized props
Use Server Actions for mutations instead of client-side API calls where possible
data.takeaway: RSC is about shipping less JavaScript, not just moving logic to the server. Place boundaries intentionally.
